newsitem.title: FRANCE: Mourning Algeria sets martyr's burial for unionist.
newsitem.headline: Mourning Algeria sets martyr's burial for unionist.

text.p: Algeria prepared a martyr's burial for assassinated trade union boss Abdelhak Benhamouda on Thursday amid a clamour of questions over whether Moslem fundamentalists or political rivals killed him.
Benhamouda's last words, "Kamel, my brother, they have betrayed us", gasped out before he died on Tuesday and reported by an Algerian newspaper, added to the mystery.
Tributes poured in from Algerian organisations and from abroad for the man known as one of Algerian President Liamine Zeroual's strongest political allies.

His million-strong Union Generale des Travailleurs Algerience (UGTA) said Benhamouda's body would lie in union headquarters from 10 a.m. (0900 GMT) on Thursday for final respects before his burial in El-Alia cemetery.
The burial place in the Algerian capital is reserved for leaders from the 1954-1962 war of independence against France and for those who have died a "martyr's" death since.

Benhamouda's final words, the ambush in the central May 1st Square and the escape in the heavily-policed city of the gunmen -- said by the government to be Moslem fundamentalists -- raised questions over his killing and its motives.
Algeria's independent newspapers all asked: "Who killed Benhamouda?", a powerful figure only in his 40s who was preparing to start his own political party.
Analysts in France who closely follow events in its former colony said Benhamouda appeared to have been killed by a rival faction within the ruling hierarchy.
One noted that Zeroual talked of having been shot by "traitors" rather than "terrorists", which is Algiers' usual official term for fundamentalists.

The independent Algerian paper Liberte asked whether Benhamouda died because he was "the new political man who was preparing...to upset the national chessboard...Who killed him, or rather, who ordered his elimination?"
The official newspaper El Moudjahid said: "It is not easy to understand this killing and the reasons which truly motivated it."
The UGTA ordered a minute's silence on Thursday and a total work stoppage except for emergency services for Saturday, the first working day of the Algerian week.
It said it would rename its headquarters after Benhamouda, who was hit by at least 14 bullets fired by four gunmen who were waiting as he left the offices for his armour-plated car.
Benhamouda, a vociferous anti-Islamist, recently expressed disillusion with Algeria's political hierarchy, saying it had done nothing to resolve five years of crisis.
About 60,000 people have been killed in the conflict which erupted in 1992 after the authorities cancelled a general election dominated by Islamists. New elections are promised before July this year.
The Algerian newspaper El Watan asked: "Who profited from this crime; a question all the world is asking."
